statement: The 350 XCF-W is KTM's single-track trail version of the 350: a six-speed gearbox, an open-cartridge WP fork with preload adjusters, the linkless PDS shock with a high-speed compression adjuster, a 2.2 gal tank, lights and a radiator fan. The street-legal EXC is the same idea with a plate; the XC-F and SX-F are the linkage bikes for tracks and GP-style races. The 2015 added an orange frame, black rims, a digital speedometer, Neken bars and Dunlop AT81 tyres and listed at $9,599.

An independent tester weighed the 2015 350 XCF-W at 241 lb empty and 255 lb fuelled, and rode over 70 miles of trail on a tank. Power is smooth and linear from low rpm to nearly 12,000, with strong torque off idle and no tendency to stall. Sixth gear is good for about 85 mph. It is jetted lean for emissions at low rpm and wants the cold-start lever when cold; the fuelling held from sea level to 8,500 ft.

An independent tester ran the 2015 350 XCF-W at 105 mm of rider sag with the clickers left stock, and found the stock settings right for riders of about 165-200 lb on trails. For sand, big whoops or motocross jumps add compression; each extra 5 mm of rear sag slows the steering and takes bite off the front. Bleed the air from the fork before riding.

Tester complaints on the 2015 350 XCF-W: the two-piece hand guards break easily, the seat foam bottoms out toward the rear under taller or heavier riders, and it is not at its best in deep whoops without stiffer settings.

The 2017 300 XC-W and 250 XC-W were all new: an engine with the crank 27 mm higher and the clutch shaft 8 mm higher, a counterbalancer shaft that cuts vibration, a new cylinder and power valve, the electric starter moved under the cases, a reworked six-speed gearbox, a diaphragm-spring hydraulic clutch, a 38 mm Mikuni TMX carburettor in place of the Keihin, a new chrome-moly frame with 22 mm offset clamps, the WP Xplor 48 fork (compression in the left leg, rebound in the right) and the WP Xplor PDS shock with a smaller 46 mm piston. A lithium battery is standard.

An independent tester weighed the 2017 300 XC-W at 224 lb empty and 239 lb with its 2.5 gal tank full. The power is smooth torque with much less vibration than before, lively into the midrange and willing to rev. List price $9,099.

The carburetted 2017-2018 XC-W runs lean and then rich as the power valve opens on its stock jetting. An independent tester found it had to be run on fresh fuel at 60:1; at 40:1 the jetting became hard to sort. A pilot in the 32.5-35 range with the needle half a clip leaner was the starting point, and an aftermarket jet kit with its own needles (one for slow trail work, one for aggressive riding) cured the hesitation. About half a turn of the power-valve adjuster changes the feel; the stock spring was preferred.

Tester notes on the 2017-2018 XC-W: the rear spring rate matters more than usual on the PDS shock (too heavy a rider and it squats, too light and it is unstable), the fork seals needed replacing after muddy rides, the lithium battery wants a short tap of the starter about 20 seconds before cranking on a cold morning, and the brakes have less outright bite and more control than the earlier bikes.

The 2016-2018 450 XC-F is the 450 SX-F of the same year with an 18 in rear wheel, a larger tank (about 2.2 gal), a side stand, hand guards, a stronger battery, softer off-road suspension settings and Dunlop AT81 tyres. It keeps the five-speed close-ratio gearbox. The 2016 has the WP 4CS fork; the 2017 changed to the WP AER 48 air fork and added the map switch with traction control.

An independent tester weighed the 450 XC-F at 232 lb empty and 245 lb full in 2016, and 230 and 241 lb in 2017. Range is about 50 miles in most conditions. Top speed is 91 mph at the rev limiter on stock gearing. It makes strong torque that hooks up rather than spins, but the light flywheel stalls easily at closed throttle and first gear is tall, so it needs re-gearing for tight trails. List price $9,999 in 2016 and $10,099 in 2017.

An independent tester's 2016 450 XC-F setup: rider sag 103-108 mm; off-road, fork compression and rebound 12-13 clicks out with the shock's compression about 5 clicks softer than standard; on a motocross track, up to 5 clicks more low-speed compression at the rear.

An independent tester's 2017 450 XC-F setup: rider sag 103-108 mm, fork with 1 psi more than standard and a few clicks of compression, shock standard with up to five more clicks of low-speed compression for motocross. The aggressive map suits good traction; the milder map with traction control suits wide-open riding on loose ground.

vals.fork: +1 psi, a few clicks more compression

statement: Tester findings on the 2016-2018 450 XC-F: it stalls at low throttle (keep a finger on the clutch), the clutch puts heat into the engine quickly and its rubber dampers should be checked every 20 hours, the stock muffler is loud and is not a spark arrestor, there is no skid plate, the hand guards are weak and the push-button fuel cap is awkward with cold hands. On two 2016 test bikes the shock piston band seized and locked the rebound.

The 2013-2015 250 XC-F is the 250 SX-F with a 2.4 gal tank, a side stand, an 18 in rear wheel, hand guards, off-road suspension valving and a six-speed semi-wide gearbox. The 2015 has the WP 4CS fork, a plain-bearing big end, a lighter clutch basket and a 22 mm front axle. List price $8,599 in 2015.

An independent tester weighed the 2015 250 XC-F at 247 lb full of fuel (about 15 lb less empty) and got almost 70 miles from a tank on a steady trail ride. On stock gearing it ran 89-90 mph. The engine revs to about 14,000 rpm with a long, flat torque curve and very little flywheel, so it stalls easily.

An independent tester's 2015 250 XC-F setup: sag 100-105 mm; for motocross stay near stock (softer springs under about 165 lb); for trail go 3-5 clicks softer on fork compression and rebound, match the shock and take half a turn off the high-speed compression. For tighter racing add a couple of teeth at the rear or drop one at the front. Bleed the fork and keep the seals wet to reduce stiction; add a skid plate and, for trail use, a spark arrestor.

vals.trail: fork 3-5 clicks softer, shock HSC 1/2 turn softer

statement: The 2019 250 XC and 300 XC are carburetted two-stroke cross-country racers built on the SX: the stiffer 2019 frame, a subframe 40 mm longer, an axle slot 5 mm longer, radiators 12 mm lower, a new pipe and silencer and new carburettor settings, with electric start, a six-speed close-ratio gearbox, a hydraulic clutch, the WP AER 48 air fork, a linkage shock, a 2.65 gal tank, an 18 in rear wheel, hand guards, a side stand and a slightly heavier flywheel than the SX. The 250 XC listed at $9,399.

An independent tester's 2019 250 XC setup: fork air 140 psi (KTM's base is 136 psi, 9.4 bar), compression 10 clicks out, rebound 15 out, shock at 105 mm sag. Stock jetting was kept with the idle turned nearly closed, on a 50/50 mix of race and pump fuel. Power valve: the aggressive (red) spring in place of the stock yellow one, with the adjuster 1-1/2 turns in from fully out. The stock suspension suits tight woods; fast, rough western terrain needs a stiffer shock spring and firmer valving. It ran over 80 mph stock.

Tester findings on the 2019 250 XC: brake pedal return springs wore out repeatedly (an aftermarket spring kit or the earlier round spring), and the fuel tap leaked into the carburettor when turned off; leaving it on reserve stopped it.

The 2016-2018 YZ450FX is the 2016 YZ450F with a five-speed wide-ratio gearbox (30% wider spread), electric start with a larger generator, its own ECU, an off-road clutch with different plates and lighter springs, 22 mm offset clamps (the 2016 YZ450F went to 25), thinner engine mounts (6 mm instead of 8), softer fork springs with cross-country valving, an 18 in rear wheel, a skid plate, an O-ring chain, a side stand and Dunlop AT81 tyres. The tank is the motocross bike's 2.0 gal. List price $8,990 in 2016.

An independent tester weighed the 2016 YZ450FX at 253 lb empty and 264 lb full. A tank lasts about 60 miles, with the last 20 uncertain. It ran 97 mph on a dry lake. The engine is snappy off the bottom and pulls to a long top end; with so little flywheel it stalls if the throttle is shut or mistimed.

An independent tester ran the 2016 YZ450FX at about 103 mm of sag (headshake creeps in near 100 mm) and, for slower trail riding, 4 clicks softer on low-speed compression at both ends. With the Power Tuner, a mellower bottom-end map improved traction and reduced stalling without costing mid or top. The frame has tabs for Yamaha's accessory radiator fan, worth fitting for tight riding; the skid plate has to come off for oil changes.

vals.trail: 4 clicks softer LSC front and rear

statement: The 2016-2018 WR450F shares the reversed-cylinder engine, five-speed wide-ratio gearbox, 22 mm offset clamps and spring rates of the YZ450FX, with a much lower first gear, heavier balance shafts, lights run from the ECU, a radiator fan, a plastic skid plate, a fuel-level sensor in the 2.0 gal tank, softer valving, a locked ECU and a quiet, restricted muffler. No hand guards are fitted. It weighed 256 lb empty and 268 lb fuelled on an independent tester's scale, about 4 lb more than the FX. List price $8,990 in 2016.

As delivered the 2016-2018 WR450F is very quiet and soft below half throttle. For closed-course use testers removed the intake baffle, replaced the throttle stop with the YZ part and took the smallest restrictor out of the muffler. Yamaha's GYTR competition kit unlocks the ECU so the Power Tuner can change fuel and ignition (map 1 aggressive, map 2 close to stock). Uncorked it revs quickly and comes close to the YZ450FX at high rpm, with less punch low down. Top speed about 95 mph; plan on 60 miles a tank.

An independent tester's 2016 WR450F setup: fork compression 13 and rebound 13 clicks out; shock low-speed compression 5 clicks from full stiff, a quarter turn more high-speed compression and rebound at 17 clicks; rear sag 100 mm (under 95 mm it became unstable). The chain slider wore out in about 20 hours.

vals.shock: LSC 5 from stiff, HSC +1/4 turn, reb 17

statement: The YZ250FX arrived for 2015 on the WR250F frame with the YZ250F engine from throttle body to muffler: a six-speed wide-ratio gearbox (lower first, taller sixth), electric start with kick backup, a 160 W alternator and extra flywheel, a clutch with lighter springs and different plates, an 18 in rear wheel, a side stand, the KYB SSS fork with a spring one step softer and softer valving, and a tank of about 2 gal. Maps can be changed with the GYTR Power Tuner. List price $7,890 in 2015.

An independent tester weighed the 2015 YZ250FX at 247.5 lb with a full tank. A tank lasted into the high 60s of miles on a desert trail ride but only around 30 miles at race pace. It ran 89 mph on stock gearing. Power is linear to a limiter near 13,000 rpm, softer off the bottom than the YZ250F and it hooks up well; the fuelling was right even at 7,500 ft.

Tester notes on the YZ250FX: the small tank limits race distance, the muffler is loud for trail use (a quiet aftermarket muffler tames it at some cost in response), the front air filter needs cleaning often in dust and roost, and it comes without hand guards or a skid plate. About 110 mm of rider sag was used in testing. The frame has a plug for an optional radiator fan.

The current RM-Z450 arrived for 2018 with new bodywork, frame and the Showa coil fork and BFRC shock. For 2019 the shock spring went from 56 to 54 N/mm with new damping, and the bike came with three plug-in couplers. Magazine testers found the 2020-2023 bikes unchanged. The engine's only updates in the previous decade were the launch and traction functions added for 2016. It is kickstart only. List price $8,999 in 2023, $600 to $2,000 less than its rivals.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

topic: RM-Z450 dyno by rpm and weight
statement: On a magazine dyno the RM-Z450 made 45.9 hp at 7,000 rpm, 52.4 hp at 8,000 rpm and peaked at 54.39 hp at 8,800-8,900 rpm, the lowest peak in the class; at 11,000 rpm it was 7.5 hp behind the Yamaha, KTM, Honda and Husqvarna. It weighed 241 lb without fuel, the heaviest 450, nearly 20 lb more than the lightest. It is brisk off the bottom and strongest from 7,000 to 8,800 rpm, then falls away above 9,000, so it is best short-shifted.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's RM-Z450 fork setup (Showa 49 mm coil): stock 0.50 kg/mm springs, compression 10 clicks out (stock 6; testers ranged from 7 to 12), rebound 12 out, legs lowered to about flush in the clamps to slow the steering and calm head shake, and 10 cc of oil added to each leg to firm the last part of the stroke.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's RM-Z450 shock setup (Showa BFRC, which has no high-speed compression adjuster): stock 54 N/mm spring, compression 1 turn out (stock 1-1/2), rebound 1 turn out (stock 3), race sag 105-108 mm, with a shock link 1 mm longer than the stock 135 mm one. The longer link lowers the high-riding rear and firms the first part of the stroke.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

statement: Stock gearing on the RM-Z450 is 13/50. Testers kept it in 2019 and later moved to 13/51 to reach third gear sooner.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

topic: RM-Z450 couplers, app and holeshot assist
statement: The RM-Z450 comes with three plug-in couplers: stock, aggressive (sharper throttle, slightly lean on top, suited to tight supercross-style tracks) and mellow. Testers raced the stock one. Suzuki's MX-Tuner 2.0 phone app adds four preset maps and custom maps with 36 editable cells; loading a map needs the connector, data cable and a separate 12 V battery. Holeshot assist (S-HAC) has three modes on the launch button.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

topic: RM-Z450 weak points and fixes from race tests
statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2018-generation RM-Z450: the clutch slips (three stiffer springs can be enough; a complete aftermarket clutch is the full cure), the chain guide wears (aftermarket guide), the 1.1 radiator cap lets it boil over (a 1.8 or 2.0 cap), the front brake is grabby with poor feel, the BFRC shock steps out when the wheels go light (a specialist rebuild, or the conventional RM-Z250 shock), the fork moves too fast in the mid-stroke then spikes (revalve), and the rear rides high, which makes it oversteer and shake at speed until it is lowered.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

topic: RM-Z450 handling and how to balance it
statement: The RM-Z450 has the sharpest turn-in of the 450s but is unstable at speed as delivered. The magazine recipe: lower the rear (the softer 2019-on spring, 105-110 mm sag and a 1 mm longer link), then slide the fork down to flush. That gives more room to tune compression, rebound and fork height. Its 2019 peak of 54.39 hp compared with 60.21 for the CRF450R, 57.51 YZ450F, 57.14 450 SX-F, 56.40 FC 450 and 55.86 KX450.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

statement: The usual answers to the RM-Z450's missing top end are an aftermarket exhaust and one more tooth on the rear sprocket; testers did not publish measured gains.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2023 Suzuki RM-Z450 race test

statement: The current RM-Z250 dates from 2019: a new head with reshaped intake ports and a more aggressive intake cam, dual injectors (one under the throttle body, one in the airbox inlet), an air-cleaner opening 30% larger, new second-gear and final ratios, a frame 0.8 lb lighter with 10% more torsional stiffness, a hex-rail aluminium subframe, a lighter swingarm, Kayaba coil-spring fork in place of the PSF-2 air fork with a Kayaba shock, a 270 mm front disc, D.I.D DirtStar rims, Dunlop MX33 tyres and footpegs moved slightly forward and up. Testers found it unchanged from 2020 through 2025. It has a five-speed gearbox and no electric start.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

topic: RM-Z250 dyno and weight against the class
statement: On a magazine dyno the RM-Z250 made 39.0 hp in 2022 and 39.52 hp in 2025, against about 44-45 hp for the KTM, Husqvarna, GasGas and Kawasaki 250s. It weighed 226-227 lb without fuel. It matches the best from 5,000 to 7,500 rpm and is friendly from about 6,000 to 9,000, then falls behind and needs short-shifting. It also vibrates more than its rivals. List price $7,899 in 2022 and $8,199 in 2025, with dealers often discounting $1,000-1,500.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2025 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

statement: The RM-Z250's stock 5.0 N/mm fork springs are too stiff for most riders. A magazine test crew's setup: 4.7-4.9 N/mm springs, compression 14 clicks out (stock 11), rebound 13 out, standard fork height. If the stock springs stay: compression fully out and the oil lowered by 20-30 in each leg, unless the rider is around 200 lb.

vals.stock_spring_fix: comp full out, oil down 20-30 per leg

source.name: Motocross Action - 2022 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's RM-Z250 shock setup: a 50 N/mm spring in place of the stock 52, race sag 107 mm (stock 105-110), high-speed compression (blue) 14 clicks out, low-speed compression (silver) 14 out, high-speed rebound (bottom) 16 out, low-speed rebound (red) 14 out. With stock springs the crew ran 104 mm of sag to put weight on the fork.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2022 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

statement: The RM-Z250 has three plug-in couplers; the white one is the most aggressive off the bottom and every magazine tester chose it, while the grey one is smoother and slower to pick up. The MX-Tuner 2.0 app has four presets (aggressive, smooth, richer, leaner) and custom maps. A tuner map written for an aftermarket exhaust ran noticeably better than stock in testing even on the stock pipe. Testers found launch control of no use on a 39 hp bike.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2025 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

topic: RM-Z250 weak points and fixes from race tests
statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2019-generation RM-Z250: clutch friction plates wear fast and it slips within a few hours of hard use (stiffer springs), the fork is supercross-stiff, the gearbox is notchy when shifted under load, the front brake is weak and fades, and it is the heaviest and least powerful bike in the class with no electric start. On the other side, testers logged 50-plus hours a year on these bikes since 2019 with no serious failures.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2025 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

topic: RM-Z250 what power mods are worth
statement: On the RM-Z250 a good full exhaust is worth about 2 hp for roughly $1,000. Testers estimated $4,000 or more in porting, cam, piston, pipe and ignition work to match a stock Austrian 250, and one heavily modified RM-Z250 only equalled a stock KX250. Aftermarket engine mounts (about $430) were tried to soften the stiff chassis feel.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2025 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test

statement: The RM-Z250 is built to turn: once the fork is softened it is the best-cornering 250 and holds a line without standing up. The cost is stability: it can oversteer on entry, tuck in tight corners and shake on fast, rough straights, and it is harsh on hard, choppy tracks with the stock fork. The cockpit is compact and suits smaller riders.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2022 Suzuki RM-Z250 race test
